screens.title: Duplicated Code & Extract Method
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll take a close look at duplicated code and the Extract Method refactoring. Duplicated code occurs when the same or very similar logic appears in two or more places in a system, which violates the DRY principle and increases maintenance cost. You will learn how to spot exact duplicates and subtle near-duplicates where variable names or surrounding code differ but the core intent is the same. We'll use Python examples to show a common pattern: repeating a member-status check in two methods, then extracting that logic into a single helper. Beyond the mechanics, I'll explain why extraction improves readability by giving a name to a behavior, and why parameterization matters when the repeated sections vary slightly. We'll also highlight common pitfalls: extracting blocks that are too large, creating new hidden dependencies, or forgetting to update all call sites. By the end you'll be able to decide when an extract is appropriate, how to parameterize it, and how to validate your refactor with quick tests. Think about a recent bug you fixed in multiple places — that's the kind of problem this refactoring prevents.

screens.title: What is Duplicated Code?
screens.narratorSegment: Duplicated code is any occurrence of the same or logically identical code in multiple places. It ranges from verbatim copies to near-duplicates where variable names, logging messages, or small surrounding steps differ but the core computation or decision is the same. Identical duplication is easier to detect with simple text search, but near-duplicates require reading for intent — for example, two methods that each decide behavior based on membership status and then perform slightly different downstream steps. In practice this smell violates the DRY principle — Don't Repeat Yourself — because a single concept or rule is implemented in more than one place. This matters because when a rule changes you must change every copy. A common concrete example is two functions checking customer tiers and applying related multipliers or discounts. If the business decides Gold members get a different multiplier, a missed update will create inconsistent behavior and elusive bugs. A misconception students often have is equating duplication solely with identical lines; instead, you must look for repeated intent. Key takeaway: think in terms of responsibilities, not text. If multiple places express the same responsibility, centralize it.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › What is Duplicated Code?
Definition

Duplicated code means repeated responsibility

This includes exact copies and near-copies that perform the same conceptual task. Detecting intent is often more important than matching lines.

Forms to watch for
  • Identical code blocks copied to another module.
  • Repeated conditional structures doing the same work with different names.
  • Near-duplicates where only logging or variable names differ.
Concrete example
Two methods each check a customer's membership and compute either points or discount using the same branching — that is duplicated intent.
Key Takeaway

Duplication is about repeated responsibility. Centralize responsibility to simplify changes and avoid inconsistent bugs.

Quick detection guide
Look for matching conditions
If two places check the same property and then act similarly, treat that as duplicated logic even if names differ.
Search for similar sequences
A repeated setup-teardown sequence around different core operations is a duplication candidate.
Misconception check
Not all repetition is harmful; brief convenience wrappers can be acceptable. Extract when the repetition represents a meaningful responsibility.

screens.title: Why duplicated code is dangerous
screens.narratorSegment: Duplicated code raises risk in three tightly related ways. First, maintenance cost increases: every copy is another place you must read and possibly change. That makes routine updates slower. Second, inconsistent fixes are a serious hazard. If you correct a bug in one spot but miss another copy, the system behaves inconsistently under different circumstances, making bugs harder to reproduce and diagnose. Third, cognitive load grows because developers must mentally track multiple implementations of the same rule. For example, if tiered pricing logic appears in two services and one is updated for a new Gold tier benefit but the other is not, customers will receive different results depending on which service handles their request. A common mistake is to treat duplication as cosmetic and only remove it when doing large rewrites; instead it's better to extract small coherent pieces early. Another misconception is that duplication only adds lines; the real cost is the multiplicative effect on change and testing effort. Key takeaway: duplication multiplies future work and multiplies the places bugs can hide. Why duplicated code is dangerous means duplication increases maintenance, risks inconsistent fixes, and raises cognitive overhead for developers.. In practical terms, maintenance cost, inconsistent fixes, and cognitive load. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Why duplicated code is dangerous
Comparison

Costs vs. benefits

Maintenance cost
More places to update means longer change cycles and higher review effort.
Inconsistent fixes
Fix one instance and miss another and you create a hard-to-find inconsistency.
Cognitive load
Developers must remember multiple implementations of the same rule when making changes.
Concrete scenario
Suppose two methods apply a member-status check for points and discount. If the business increases Gold multipliers and you only update one method, customers will see different outcomes depending on which calculation runs. This inconsistency can erode trust and complicate debugging.
Misconception
Believing duplication is only a cosmetic issue. In reality its cost compounds as the project grows and requirements change.
Key Takeaway

Treat duplication as a functional risk that should be addressed early with small, test-backed refactors.

screens.title: Extract Method — basic steps
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Method is a focused refactoring: select a coherent chunk of code, give it a clear name, move it into a new method, and replace the original occurrences with calls. The safest approach is small steps. First, identify the repeated responsibility and ensure it represents a single concept. Second, copy the block into a new private helper with a name that expresses intent — if naming is hard, the chunk may be doing too much. Third, determine what varies between occurrences and add parameters for those varying pieces. Fourth, replace the original code with calls to the new helper in every location, and run tests after each replacement. Fifth, remove the original duplicated code. Throughout, keep changes minimal and run your test suite or simple asserts at each step. A common pitfall is extracting an overly large block that still contains multiple responsibilities; that increases the chance of behavior change and makes naming difficult. Key takeaway: make each extraction an atomic, testable step and prefer many small, verified extractions over a single large one. Extract Method — basic steps means select a coherent block, name it for intent, parameterize differences, replace calls everywhere, and verify with tests.. In practical terms, a safe, repeatable checklist for extracting logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Extract Method — basic steps
Process Flow

A safe, repeatable checklist

1. Identify
Find repeated responsibility with the same intent.
2. Name
Choose a name that describes what it does, not how.
3. Parameterize
Pass varying data as arguments.
4. Replace
Update all call sites and run tests.
5. Remove
Delete old copies once verified.
Example rule
Two methods check membership tiers, compute multipliers, and log messages. Extract the membership-decoding logic into a helper that returns multipliers for points and discount rate.
Common mistake
Extracting a chunk that still mixes responsibilities. If you struggle to name the new method clearly, split the chunk and extract smaller pieces.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Before: Customer class
Code example
class Customer:
    def __init__(self, name, member_status, purchases):
        self.name = name
        self.member_status = member_status  # 'Gold', 'Silver', 'Bronze'
        self.purchases = purchases  # list of amounts

    def calculate_loyalty_points(self):
        if self.member_status == 'Gold':
            print(f"[{self.name}] Gold member - calculating points with bonus.")
            points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.15
        elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
            print(f"[{self.name}] Silver member - calculating points.")
            points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.10
        else:
            print(f"[{self.name}] Standard member - calculating points.")
            points = sum(self.purchases) * 0.05
        return points

    def apply_discount(self, total_amount):
        discount_rate = 0.0
        if self.member_status == 'Gold':
            print(f"[{self.name}] Gold member - applying 20% discount.")
            discount_rate = 0.20
        elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
            print(f"[{self.name}] Silver member - applying 10% discount.")
            discount_rate = 0.10
        else:
            print(f"[{self.name}] Standard member - no discount.")
            discount_rate = 0.0
        return total_amount * (1 - discount_rate)
What to notice
  • Both methods repeat the if/elif/else membership check.
  • Values for multipliers and rates are inline in each branch.
  • Print messages differ slightly but the decision tree is the same.
Example insight
This is a classic extract candidate: centralize the membership decoding so callers are simpler and consistent.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › After: Extracting helper
Refactored code
class Customer:
    def __init__(self, name, member_status, purchases):
        self.name = name
        self.member_status = member_status
        self.purchases = purchases

    def _get_member_status_details(self):
        if self.member_status == 'Gold':
            return 'Gold', 0.15, 0.20
        elif self.member_status == 'Silver':
            return 'Silver', 0.10, 0.10
        else:
            return 'Standard', 0.05, 0.0

    def calculate_loyalty_points(self):
        status_name, points_multiplier, _ = self._get_member_status_details()
        print(f"[{self.name}] {status_name} member - calculating points.")
        return sum(self.purchases) * points_multiplier

    def apply_discount(self, total_amount):
        status_name, _, discount_rate = self._get_member_status_details()
        print(f"[{self.name}] {status_name} member - applying {discount_rate*100}% discount.")
        return total_amount * (1 - discount_rate)
Why this helps
One place to change membership rules and the name _get_member_status_details communicates the intent of decoding tier details.
Parameter choices
The helper returns only the values callers need; unused parts can be ignored with placeholders like underscore.
Key Takeaway

A well-scoped helper reduces duplication and concentrates business rules in one place for easier maintenance.

screens.title: Parameterizing extracted methods
screens.narratorSegment: Not every duplicated block is identical; sometimes the repeated code differs by context or a small variable. Parameterization means passing the varying parts as arguments so the extracted method remains general. For example, if one caller needs a different print message or an additional context string, pass a context argument rather than embedding the message inside the helper. Another option is to return data and let callers format their own message. The principle is to avoid making the helper depend on too many external variables from its original context. A common error is to reach back into the caller's environment rather than exposing required data via parameters; that creates hidden dependencies and reduces reuse. When parameterizing, prefer explicit parameter names that describe what the value is, not where it came from. If you find yourself with a long parameter list, consider grouping related values into a small object. Key takeaway: parameterization preserves reuse and keeps the helper focused on one responsibility while allowing controlled variation. Parameterizing extracted methods means pass varying parts as parameters or return raw data for callers to format, keeping helpers reusable and free of hidden dependencies.. In practical terms, make the helper flexible for slightly different callers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pattern

Pass what varies, return what is shared

Two parameter approaches

screens.title: Common mistakes when extracting
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Method is powerful but easy to misuse. One common error is extracting too little — moving a single line that doesn't represent a coherent responsibility. That yields a helper whose name is meaningless and adds indirection without clarity. Another error is extracting too much: moving a large block that mixes responsibilities makes the helper hard to reason about and more likely to break behavior. Poorly named methods are also a trap; if you cannot name the new method succinctly, that signals it does too much. Hidden dependencies occur when the extracted method reaches into the caller's context rather than accepting required data as parameters. This introduces tight coupling and can create Feature Envy, where the helper depends on many external details. The safety practice is small steps with tests: extract a clear chunk, run tests, then replace each call site and run tests again. If tests fail, revert and examine the extraction boundary. Key takeaway: nameable, single-responsibility extractions are safe; everything else needs further decomposition before extraction. Too little
Extracting a single line or trivial statement creates noise without clarity. Nameability is a good filter.
Too much

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Refactoring duplicated configuration
Starter code
# settings_manager.py
class SettingsManager:
    def __init__(self, environment):
        self.environment = environment
        self.settings = {}

    def load_database_settings(self):
        if self.environment == 'development':
            self.settings['db_host'] = 'localhost'
            self.settings['db_port'] = 5432
            self.settings['db_user'] = 'dev_user'
            self.settings['db_password'] = 'dev_pass'
        elif self.environment == 'staging':
            self.settings['db_host'] = 'staging.db.example.com'
            # ...other staging values...
        elif self.environment == 'production':
            self.settings['db_host'] = 'prod.db.example.com'
            # ...other prod values...

    def load_api_keys(self):
        if self.environment == 'development':
            self.settings['api_key_weather'] = 'dev_weather_key'
            self.settings['api_key_maps'] = 'dev_maps_key'
        elif self.environment == 'staging':
            # ...staging keys...
            pass
        elif self.environment == 'production':
            # ...prod keys...
            pass
Identify duplication
Both load methods switch on the same environment; that dispatch is the repeated logic to extract.
Refactor suggestion
Create _get_env_settings(kind) that returns a dict for 'database' or 'api_keys' and merge it into self.settings.
Verification
Use simple asserts after loader calls to confirm keys and values match expected environment outputs.

screens.title: How to verify behavior after refactoring
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring must preserve external behavior. The recommended workflow is: make one small extraction, run your tests, then replace the next call site and run tests again. For practical verification in small examples, write simple asserts that compare outputs before and after the change. For example, after extracting the membership helper, assert that calculating loyalty points for a Gold customer returns the same numeric value and that the discount calculation produces the same result. In the SettingsManager scenario, assert that settings contain specific host and port keys for each environment. If you use a test framework, write unit tests that exercise both old and refactored paths during the refactor and run them frequently. If tests fail, immediately revert the last change and inspect the extraction boundary. A common misconception is assuming manual smoke checks are sufficient; automated asserts reduce human error and let you refactor quickly and confidently. Key takeaway: incrementally extract and verify with fast, focused tests so behavior remains unchanged throughout the process. Process

screens.title: Limits of Extract Method and alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Method is not the universal solution. There are times when extraction is the wrong move. If the repeated logic depends heavily on internal state of the original object, extracting it into a separate helper may create awkward parameter lists or reveal Feature Envy — a smell where a piece of logic seems to belong to another class. In those cases, consider Extract Class or moving behavior to a more appropriate object. If the duplication is a small one-line convenience that improves readability, extracting it may add indirection without benefit. Also, if two sections are only superficially similar but differ in subtle business rules, extracting a shared helper may force unnatural parameterization that hides important differences. The practical rule is: extract when you can give the helper a clear name and keep call sites readable. Alternatives include Extract Class, introducing a small value object, or leaving short, expressive duplication until a better abstraction emerges. Key takeaway: prefer extractions that express a single responsibility and consider other refactorings when extraction would force awkward coupling. Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › When to avoid extraction
Comparison & Alternatives
Signs extraction may be wrong
  • The helper needs many parameters from the caller.
  • The logic more naturally belongs to another class (Feature Envy).
  • Call sites become noisier or less readable.
Alternative refactors
  • Extract Class: move related behavior into a new class.
  • Introduce a small value object for grouped parameters.
  • Delay extraction until a clearer abstraction emerges for complex differences.
Reflective question

If you extract and then need to pass many parameters or move most of an object's state, ask whether the new method actually belongs to a different class.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials. First, duplicated code includes identical and near-identical logic; look for repeated responsibility rather than exact text matches. Second, DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself — is the guiding principle: a single source of truth reduces the places you must change when rules evolve. Third, Extract Method centralizes repeated logic into a named helper, improving readability and maintainability. When extracting, parameterize differences and prefer returning data rather than hidden side-effects. Use small steps and tests to verify behavior after each change. Avoid extracting code that is too large, has multiple responsibilities, or introduces hidden dependencies. If extraction forces many parameters or feature envy, consider alternatives like Extract Class or small value objects. The core payoff is simpler maintenance: one place to update business rules and fewer opportunities for inconsistent bugs. Keep these concepts in mind as practical heuristics when you spot duplication in your code.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll take a close look at duplicated code and the Extract Method refactoring. Duplicated code occurs when the same or very similar logic appears in two or more places in a system, which violates the DRY principle and increases maintenance cost. You will learn how to spot exact duplicates and subtle near-duplicates where variable names or surrounding code differ but the core intent is the same. We'll use Python examples to show a common pattern: repeating a member-status check in two methods, then extracting that logic into a single helper. Beyond the mechanics, I'll explain why extraction improves readability by giving a name to a behavior, and why parameterization matters when the repeated sections vary slightly. We'll also highlight common pitfalls: extracting blocks that are too large, creating new hidden dependencies, or forgetting to update all call sites. By the end you'll be able to decide when an extract is appropriate, how to parameterize it, and how to validate your refactor with quick tests. Think about a recent bug you fixed in multiple places — that's the kind of problem this refactoring prevents.

In the next few screens we'll make concrete learning goals you can use to measure progress. First, you'll learn to recognize various forms of duplicated code. That includes identical blocks, repeated conditional structures, and near-duplicates that only differ by names or small variations. A clear detection skill helps you avoid surface-level fixes that leave duplication. Second, you'll be able to explain why duplication hurts maintainability: more lines to read, more places to change, and higher risk of inconsistent bug fixes. Third, you'll apply the Extract Method refactoring to move repeated logic into a single helper, which centralizes behavior and helps readability. Fourth, you'll practice parameterizing extracted methods so they accept the parts that vary, keeping one reusable implementation. Each of these objectives pairs a practical skill with the reasoning behind it, so you both do the refactor and understand why it reduces risk. During the exercises you will write small tests and check behavior, reinforcing the safety-first approach to refactoring.

This second set of objectives focuses on safe refactoring habits and verification. First, you'll learn to take small, test-backed steps when extracting a method. That means extract a single coherent concept, run tests, and then continue. Second, you'll learn to name extracted methods clearly so the method communicates intent rather than implementation details. Third, you will practice spotting common extraction errors: extracting too much, leaving hidden dependencies, or introducing feature envy by making the helper rely on too many external variables. Finally, you'll master verifying your refactor by running quick automated checks or simple asserts that confirm external behavior didn't change. These objectives emphasize not just the act of extracting, but doing it in a disciplined, reversible way so you never leave the codebase in a broken state. The combination of small steps, clear names, and verification will make refactors trustworthy and low-risk.

Duplicated code is any occurrence of the same or logically identical code in multiple places. It ranges from verbatim copies to near-duplicates where variable names, logging messages, or small surrounding steps differ but the core computation or decision is the same. Identical duplication is easier to detect with simple text search, but near-duplicates require reading for intent — for example, two methods that each decide behavior based on membership status and then perform slightly different downstream steps. In practice this smell violates the DRY principle — Don't Repeat Yourself — because a single concept or rule is implemented in more than one place. This matters because when a rule changes you must change every copy. A common concrete example is two functions checking customer tiers and applying related multipliers or discounts. If the business decides Gold members get a different multiplier, a missed update will create inconsistent behavior and elusive bugs. A misconception students often have is equating duplication solely with identical lines; instead, you must look for repeated intent. Key takeaway: think in terms of responsibilities, not text. If multiple places express the same responsibility, centralize it.

Duplicated code raises risk in three tightly related ways. First, maintenance cost increases: every copy is another place you must read and possibly change. That makes routine updates slower. Second, inconsistent fixes are a serious hazard. If you correct a bug in one spot but miss another copy, the system behaves inconsistently under different circumstances, making bugs harder to reproduce and diagnose. Third, cognitive load grows because developers must mentally track multiple implementations of the same rule. For example, if tiered pricing logic appears in two services and one is updated for a new Gold tier benefit but the other is not, customers will receive different results depending on which service handles their request. A common mistake is to treat duplication as cosmetic and only remove it when doing large rewrites; instead it's better to extract small coherent pieces early. Another misconception is that duplication only adds lines; the real cost is the multiplicative effect on change and testing effort. Key takeaway: duplication multiplies future work and multiplies the places bugs can hide. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Extract Method is a focused refactoring: select a coherent chunk of code, give it a clear name, move it into a new method, and replace the original occurrences with calls. The safest approach is small steps. First, identify the repeated responsibility and ensure it represents a single concept. Second, copy the block into a new private helper with a name that expresses intent — if naming is hard, the chunk may be doing too much. Third, determine what varies between occurrences and add parameters for those varying pieces. Fourth, replace the original code with calls to the new helper in every location, and run tests after each replacement. Fifth, remove the original duplicated code. Throughout, keep changes minimal and run your test suite or simple asserts at each step. A common pitfall is extracting an overly large block that still contains multiple responsibilities; that increases the chance of behavior change and makes naming difficult. Key takeaway: make each extraction an atomic, testable step and prefer many small, verified extractions over a single large one. Extract Method is not the universal solution. There are times when extraction is the wrong move. If the repeated logic depends heavily on internal state of the original object, extracting it into a separate helper may create awkward parameter lists or reveal Feature Envy — a smell where a piece of logic seems to belong to another class. In those cases, consider Extract Class or moving behavior to a more appropriate object. If the duplication is a small one-line convenience that improves readability, extracting it may add indirection without benefit. Also, if two sections are only superficially similar but differ in subtle business rules, extracting a shared helper may force unnatural parameterization that hides important differences. The practical rule is: extract when you can give the helper a clear name and keep call sites readable. Let's summarize the essentials. First, duplicated code includes identical and near-identical logic; look for repeated responsibility rather than exact text matches. Second, DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself — is the guiding principle: a single source of truth reduces the places you must change when rules evolve. Third, Extract Method centralizes repeated logic into a named helper, improving readability and maintainability. When extracting, parameterize differences and prefer returning data rather than hidden side-effects. Use small steps and tests to verify behavior after each change. Avoid extracting code that is too large, has multiple responsibilities, or introduces hidden dependencies. If extraction forces many parameters or feature envy, consider alternatives like Extract Class or small value objects. The core payoff is simpler maintenance: one place to update business rules and fewer opportunities for inconsistent bugs. Keep these concepts in mind as practical heuristics when you spot duplication in your code.

A few practical heuristics will help you act in real code. First, prefer extraction when a repeated responsibility can be named clearly. Second, make varying parts explicit via parameters or returned data instead of implicit dependencies. Third, extract in small steps and run fast tests after each change; if tests fail, revert and re-evaluate. Fourth, avoid extracting blocks that grab many variables from their original scope — that creates hidden coupling. Fifth, when extraction would force awkward parameters or indicate the logic belongs elsewhere, consider alternatives like Extract Class. These rules will guide sensible refactors: favor clarity, small steps, and verification. Ask yourself after each extraction: can I name it? Can I test it easily? If the answers are yes, you're probably making the code safer and easier to change.
